newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Defector wins Manila asylum but stays in shadows.
newsitem.headline: Defector wins Manila asylum but stays in shadows.

text.p: Officials kept a veil of secrecy around the whereabouts of North Korea's highest-ranking defector on Thursday more than two days after Philippine President Fidel Ramos gave him temporary asylum with assurances of utmost protection.

Mindful of the threat of assassins, officials maintained a total news blackout around Hwang Jang-yop as Manila and Seoul negotiated behind the scenes on how long he would stay on Philippine soil before he flies to South Korea.
In giving Hwang temporary haven, Ramos on Wednesday made it clear that he could stay in the country "only for as long as necessary and as short as possible."

Hwang, a top aide to North Korea's senior leader Kim Jong-il, arrived at the former U.S. Clark airbase north of Manila on Tuesday after waiting for nearly five weeks in a South Korean consulate in Beijing.

Despite the Philippines' reputation as a free-wheeling democracy where anything of news value cannot stay secret for long, a Philippine presidential task force has successfully kept from the public the location of Hwang's hideaway.
Ramos was clearly piqued at his news conference on Thursday when reporters kept pressing him for information about the defector.
"No comment. The security of our visitor is of paramount importance," Ramos said, brushing aside further questions.
North Korea has a history of deadly attacks against arch-rival South Korea with which it is still frozen in Cold War confrontation.
Three days after Hwang sought asylum in Beijing, a North Korean defector was fatally shot near Seoul, found by assassins despite having undergone cosmetic surgery to hide his identity.
The victim, Li Il-nam, was a nephew of Kim Jong-il.

Security sources earlier said Hwang might stay in the Philippines for a week, but South Korea's Yonyhap news agency quoted a Seoul foreign ministry spokesman as saying he might remain in his present haven for "much longer than 10 days."
The official did not rule out shortening Hwang's Philippine sojourn if the situation changed, the agency said.

In Manila, a senior official at the Department of Foreign Affairs told reporters on Wednesday that China and South Korea had failed to reach agreement on the number of days Hwang would have to stay in the Philippines.
The official said this matter was now being discussed between Manila and Seoul.
"In giving asylum to Hwang, the government has advanced our national interests by helping break a diplomatic impasse," the Philippine Daily Inquirer said in an editorial on Thursday.

"The formula into which the Philippines was drawn again shows the Asian genius for compromise that not only saves faces but also accommodates Asian sensitivity to avoid confrontation," the newspaper said.
Other analysts said the Philippines stood to reap a diplomatic bonanza in accepting Hwang.

By helping China out of a tricky situation, the Philippines gains leverage in future relations with its giant neighbour in their territorial dispute over the potentially oil-rich Spratly Islands in the South China Sea, the analysts said.
But Max Soliven, publisher and columnist of the Philippine Star newspaper, wrote that the sooner Hwang left for Seoul, the better it would be for Manila.

North Koreans "may be facing famine, starvation has afflicted the once-militant and aggressive country, but they haven't lost their skills at armed infiltration and espionage," Soliven said. "A hit team...could already be on the way."
